library(pacman)

```{r echo=FALSE}
# Table styling
style_table <- function(tbl) {
  tbl %>%
    kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")) %>%
    row_spec(0, bold = TRUE, color = "white", background = "#2B1231")
}

# Colour palette and chart theme
deeppurple  <- "#2B1231"
lavender  <- "#b19cd9"
coral <- "#E76F51"
purple <- "#69359c"

# Number formatters: usd0 = whole dollars, usd2 = dollars and cents, big = thousands separators
usd0 <- scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)
usd2 <- scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 0.01)
big  <- scales::label_comma()

theme_report <- theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title         = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, colour = "#2B1231"),
    plot.subtitle      = element_text(colour = purple),
    plot.caption       = element_text(colour = "grey50", hjust = 0),
    axis.title         = element_text(colour = purple),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.margin        = margin(12, 16, 12, 12)
  )
```

# 1. Background

Retailers often invest in **direct-marketing campaigns**, such as
coupons. Households are given coupons as part of these marketing scheme
but the question is:

> Do these campaigns increase household spend, and do all household
> types respond in the same way?

This first four sections of this project explain the data, check its
quality, describe how households shop and the campaigns looked at in
this analysis. Later sections will measure the effect of the campaigns
themselves. Each section follows the same pattern: what we look at, what
we found, and what it means for the campaign analysis.

## About the data

The data covers two years of grocery shopping by 2500 households who
shop regularly at one U.S. retailer. It records every product they
bought, as well as which households were targeted by 30 direct-marketing
campaigns and which coupons were redeemed.

```{r reading-in-data}
#| message: false
# Reading in the data
transactions  <- read_csv("data/raw/transaction_data.csv") %>% 
  clean_names()
products      <- read_csv("data/raw/product.csv") %>% 
  clean_names()
demographics  <- read_csv("data/raw/hh_demographic.csv") %>% 
  clean_names()
campaign_desc <- read_csv("data/raw/campaign_desc.csv") %>% 
  clean_names()
campaign_hh   <- read_csv("data/raw/campaign_table.csv") %>% 
  clean_names()
redemptions   <- read_csv("data/raw/coupon_redempt.csv") %>% 
  clean_names()
```

Six data sets are examined in this analysis. The transactions data set
is the core of the analysis. It contains one row for every product on
every receipt. The other data sets describe the products, households and
campaigns, and link to it through shared IDs such as `household_key` and
`product_id`.

```{r data-sets-used}
# Data set summary
tables_used <- tibble(
  Table = c("transactions", "products", "demographics",
            "campaign_desc", "campaign_hh", "redemptions"),
  `What it holds` = c(
    "Every product bought, one row per product per receipt",
    "Product details such as department and brand",
    "Age, income and household size (some households only)",
    "The 30 campaigns and their start and end days",
    "Which households were targeted by which campaign",
    "Which households redeemed a coupon, and when"
  ),
  Rows = big(c(nrow(transactions), nrow(products), nrow(demographics),
               nrow(campaign_desc), nrow(campaign_hh), nrow(redemptions)))
)

# Display in kable
tables_used %>%
  kable(caption = "The six data sets used in this report", align = c("l", "l", "r")) %>%
  style_table()
```

### Key terms

- **Household:** one shopping household, identified by a household key.
- **Basket:** one shopping trip. All line items bought together share
  the same basket ID.
- **Line item:** one product on one receipt. Each row of the
  transactions table is a line item.
- **Campaign:** a direct-marketing effort sent to chosen households,
  usually with coupons.

### Variables in the transactions data set

The two key variable sin the `transactions` data set are `sales_value`
(the money received for a line) and `quantity` (the number of units
bought). Two units of a \$1.50 item is a quantity of 2 and a sales value
of about \$3.00. Spend in this report is measured with sales value.
Below is a table summarising key variables from the `transactions` data
set.

```{r variable-dictionary}
# What each column in the transactions table means
variable_dictionary <- tibble(
  Variable = c("household_key", "basket_id", "day", "week_no", "product_id",
               "store_id", "quantity", "sales_value", "retail_disc",
               "coupon_disc", "coupon_match_disc", "trans_time"),
  Meaning = c(
    "Unique ID for the household that shopped",
    "Unique ID for one shopping trip; links all items bought together",
    "Day of the purchase, counted from the start of the data",
    "Week of the purchase, counted from the start of the data",
    "Unique ID for the product; links to the products table",
    "Store where the purchase was made",
    "Number of units of that product bought on that line",
    "Money the retailer received for that line, in dollars",
    "Discount from the retailer's loyalty-card programme (stored as a negative number)",
    "Discount from a manufacturer coupon",
    "Discount from the retailer matching a manufacturer coupon",
    "Time of day of the purchase on a 24-hour clock (1631 = 4:31 pm)"
  )
)

# Display in kable
variable_dictionary %>%
  kable(caption = "Variable dictionary: transactions table") %>%
  style_table()
```

# 2. Data Quality

Before describing or analysing the data, it was checked that it is
complete, free of duplicates and free of values that would distort the
results.

## Missingness

First the data was examined for missingness.

```{r data-quality-missingness}
# Count missing values in each column
missing_wide <- transactions %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x))))

# Turn the wide row into a long table, one row per column
missing_long <- missing_wide %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = everything(),
    names_to  = "Column",
    values_to = "Missing values"
  )

# Display in kable
missing_long %>%
  kable(caption = "Missing values per column in the transactions table") %>%
  style_table()

```

Across all 12 columns of the `transactions` data set, all columns have 0
rows containing missing data.

## Duplications

Next we examined the transaction data set for rows that were duplicates.

```{r data-quality-duplicate-rows}
# Count of any duplicate rows
n_duplicates <- sum(duplicated(transactions))

cat("Number of duplicate rows:", n_duplicates, "\n")
```

The `transactions` data set contained **`r (n_duplicates)`** duplicate
rows.

## Data counts

The next table shows the counts of key variables in the transaction data
set.

```{r data-quality-data-counts}
# Counts of people, baskets, products, stores, time
data_counts <- transactions %>% 
  summarise(
    households = n_distinct(household_key),
    baskets    = n_distinct(basket_id),
    products   = n_distinct(product_id),
    stores     = n_distinct(store_id),
    first_day  = min(day),
    last_day   = max(day),
    first_week = min(week_no),
    last_week  = max(week_no)
  )

# Turn the wide row into a long table, one row per column
data_counts_long <- data_counts %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = everything(),
    names_to  = "Column",
    values_to = "Data Counts"
  )

# Display in kable
data_counts_long %>%
  kable(caption = "Counts of key variables from the transaction dataset") %>%
  style_table() 
```

The data covers **`r big(data_counts$households)`** households,
**`r big(data_counts$baskets)`** shopping trips and
**`r big(data_counts$products)`** different products across
**`r data_counts$stores`** stores. It runs for
**`r data_counts$last_week`** weeks (`r data_counts$last_day` days).

## Sales and quantity values

Checks for zero or negative sales and zero quantities, which can distort
spend totals..

```{r}
# Sales and quantity values
sales_quantity_values <- transactions %>% 
  summarise(
    zero_sales             = sum(sales_value == 0),
    negative_value_sales   = sum(sales_value < 0),
    zero_quantity          = sum(quantity == 0),
    min_sales              = min(sales_value),
    max_sales              = max(sales_value)
  )

# Turn the wide row into a long table, one row per column
sales_quantity_values_wide <- sales_quantity_values %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = everything(),
    names_to  = "Column",
    values_to = "Values"
  )

# Display in kable
sales_quantity_values_wide %>%
  kable(caption = "Sales and quantity values") %>%
  style_table() 
```

There are no negative sales values, so no returns or refunds are
recorded as negative sales. However,
**`r big(sales_quantity_values$zero_sales)`** lines
(`r scales::percent(sales_quantity_values$zero_sales / nrow(transactions), accuracy = 0.01)`
of all lines) have a sales value of zero, and
**`r big(sales_quantity_values$zero_quantity)`** lines
(`r scales::percent(sales_quantity_values$zero_quantity / nrow(transactions), accuracy = 0.01)`)
have a quantity of zero.

**What this means for the analysis:**

- **Spend:** Lines with zero sales add nothing to a household's total
  spend, so they don't distort spend totals.
- **Averages per line:** They do pull the average line value down
  slightly, because they count as lines. Household and basket totals are
  not affected.
- **Units:** A quantity of zero can't be used to work out a price per
  unit, because dividing by zero gives an error. Quantity is not used
  for that in this report.
- **Scale:** Both groups are under 1% of the data, so the main results
  are very unlikely to change. These rows are kept in, and flagged here
  for transparency.

## Demographic coverage

Shows how many shoppers have demographic details, which limits every
analysis by age, income or household size to that subset.

```{r demographic-coverage}
# What share of shoppers have demographic information?
households_in_transactions <- n_distinct(transactions$household_key)
households_in_demographics <- n_distinct(demographics$household_key)

# Households with demographic details, and the share of all households
cat("Households in the transactions data:", households_in_transactions, "\n")
cat("Households with demographic details:", households_in_demographics, "\n")
cat("Share with demographic details:", scales::percent(households_in_demographics / households_in_transactions, accuracy = 0.1), "\n")

```

Only **`r households_in_demographics`** of
**`r big(households_in_transactions)`** households
(`r scales::percent(households_in_demographics / households_in_transactions, accuracy = 1)`)
have demographic details. Any breakdown by age, income or household size
describes this group only, not all shoppers.

# 3. Descriptive Statistics

This section describes how much households buy and how much their
spending varies. In the tables, **Mean (SD)** is the average with the
spread around it, and **Median** is the middle value. When a few large
values pull the mean up, the median is a better picture of a typical
case.

## Line-item summary

Summarises the size and spread of each purchase line, which shows how
skewed spending is before any grouping.

```{r line-item-summary}
# Put sales and quantity in one long column so we can summarise both at once
line_item_summary <- transactions %>%
  select(sales_value, quantity) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Value") %>%
  group_by(Variable) %>%
  summarise(
    `Mean (SD)` = paste0(round(mean(Value), 2), " (", round(sd(Value), 2), ")"),
    Median      = round(median(Value), 2),
    Min         = min(Value),
    Max         = max(Value)
  )

# Display in kable
line_item_summary %>%
  kable(caption = "Line-item summary: sales value and quantity") %>%
  style_table() 
```

The typical line item is worth
**`r usd2(median(transactions$sales_value))`** (median), and the average
is **`r usd2(mean(transactions$sales_value))`** (SD
`r usd2(sd(transactions$sales_value))`). The average is higher because a
few expensive items pull it up. Quantity is more extreme: a few lines
record very large quantities (the largest is
`r big(max(transactions$quantity))` units). Because of this, quantity is
not used in this report and spend is measured with sales value.

## Household totals

Builds one row per household (total spend, number of trips, average
basket value), because most later analyses compare households, not
single purchases. Most of the later analysis compares households, so
each household's purchases are added up into a single row.

```{r household-totals}
# Total sales value and number of baskets for each household
household_totals <- transactions %>%
  group_by(household_key) %>%
  summarise(
    total_spend = sum(sales_value),
    trips       = n_distinct(basket_id)
  ) %>%
  mutate(avg_basket_value = total_spend / trips)   # average spend per trip

# Show the first five households as a check
household_totals %>%
  head(5) %>%
  mutate(
    total_spend      = usd2(total_spend),
    avg_basket_value = usd2(avg_basket_value)
  ) %>%
  kable(caption = "First five households",
        col.names = c("Household", "Total spend", "Trips", "Average basket value"),
        align = c("l", "r", "r", "r")) %>%
  style_table()
```

- **Total spend:** everything the household spent over the two years.
- **Trips:** the number of separate shopping trips (baskets).
- **Average basket value:** total spend divided by trips.

A typical household spent
**`r usd0(median(household_totals$total_spend))`** over the two years
(median), made **`r median(household_totals$trips)`** trips and spent
**`r usd2(median(household_totals$avg_basket_value))`** per trip.
Average spend is higher, at
**`r usd0(mean(household_totals$total_spend))`** (SD
`r usd0(sd(household_totals$total_spend))`), and the SD is almost as
large as the mean. Households vary a lot: some shop far more than
others.

## Household summary

Shows the typical household's spend, trips and basket size, with how
much they vary, which sets the baseline for judging campaign effects.

```{r household-summary}
# Same summary as before, now at household level
household_summary <- household_totals %>%
  select(total_spend, trips, avg_basket_value) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Value") %>%
  group_by(Variable) %>%
  summarise(
    `Mean (SD)` = paste0(round(mean(Value), 2), " (", round(sd(Value), 2), ")"),
    Median      = round(median(Value), 2),
    Min         = round(min(Value), 2),
    Max         = round(max(Value), 2)
  )

# Display in kable
household_summary %>%
  kable(caption = "Household summary") %>%
  style_table() 
```

A typical household spent
**`r usd0(median(household_totals$total_spend))`** over the two years
(median), made **`r median(household_totals$trips)`** trips and spent
**`r usd2(median(household_totals$avg_basket_value))`** per trip.
Average spend is higher, at
**`r usd0(mean(household_totals$total_spend))`** (SD
`r usd0(sd(household_totals$total_spend))`), and the SD is almost as
large as the mean. Households vary a lot, meaning some shop far more
than others.

### Distribution of household spend

A typical household spent
**`r usd0(median(household_totals$total_spend))`** over the two years
(median). The chart shows whether most households spend a similar amount
or a few spend far more. If the mean sits to the right of the median, a
few heavy spenders are pulling the average up.

```{r household-spend-histogram}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
# Summary numbers used to label the chart
spend_mean   <- mean(household_totals$total_spend)
spend_sd     <- sd(household_totals$total_spend)
spend_median <- median(household_totals$total_spend)
spend_min    <- min(household_totals$total_spend)
spend_max    <- max(household_totals$total_spend)

household_totals %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = total_spend)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = lavender, colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = spend_median, colour = deeppurple, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = spend_mean, colour = coral, linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = spend_median, y = Inf, hjust = 1.08, vjust = 1.6,
           label = paste0("Median: ", usd0(spend_median)),
           colour = deeppurple, fontface = "bold", size = 4.2) +
  annotate("text", x = spend_mean, y = Inf, hjust = -0.08, vjust = 1.6,
           label = paste0("Mean: ", usd0(spend_mean), " (SD ", usd0(spend_sd), ")"),
           colour = coral, fontface = "bold", size = 4.2) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.2, 0.05)),labels = usd0) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = big, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.08))) +
  labs(
    title    = "Total spend per household over two years",
    subtitle = paste0("Range: ", usd0(spend_min), " to ", usd0(spend_max),
                      " across ", big(nrow(household_totals)), " households"),
    x        = "Total spend over two years",
    y        = "Number of households",
    caption  = "Solid line = median; dashed line = mean."
  ) +
  theme_report
```

Most households sit at the lower end, with a long tail of heavy spenders
reaching **`r usd0(spend_max)`**. The mean (dashed line) sits to the
right of the median (solid line), which confirms the skew. For the
campaign analysis, this means comparing each household with itself
before and during a campaign is fairer than comparing different
households with each other.

### Distribution of basket value

Shows how much a typical shopping trip is worth, and how skewed trip
size is.

```{r basket-value-histogram}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5.5
# Total value of each basket (one shopping trip)
basket_values <- transactions %>%
  group_by(basket_id) %>%
  summarise(basket_value = sum(sales_value))

# Summary numbers use ALL baskets
basket_mean   <- mean(basket_values$basket_value)
basket_sd     <- sd(basket_values$basket_value)
basket_median <- median(basket_values$basket_value)
basket_min    <- min(basket_values$basket_value)
basket_max    <- max(basket_values$basket_value)

# Cut off the top 1% of baskets in the chart only, so a few huge baskets do not squash it
cutoff <- quantile(basket_values$basket_value, 0.99)

basket_values %>%
  filter(basket_value <= cutoff) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = basket_value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = lavender, colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = basket_median, colour = deeppurple, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = basket_mean, colour = coral, linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = basket_median, y = Inf, hjust = 1.08, vjust = 1.6,
           label = paste0("Median: ", usd2(basket_median)),
           colour = deeppurple, fontface = "bold", size = 4.2) +
  annotate("text", x = basket_mean, y = Inf, hjust = -0.08, vjust = 1.6,
           label = paste0("Mean: ", usd2(basket_mean), " (SD ", usd2(basket_sd), ")"),
           colour = coral, fontface = "bold", size = 4.2) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.2, 0.05)), labels = usd0) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = big, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.08))) +
  labs(
    title    = "Value of each shopping trip",
    subtitle = paste0("All ", big(nrow(basket_values)), " baskets range from ",
                      usd2(basket_min), " to ", usd2(basket_max),
                      ". The chart hides the top 1% (above ", usd0(cutoff), ")."),
    x        = "Basket value",
    y        = "Number of baskets",
    caption  = "Solid line = median; dashed line = mean. Mean, SD and range use all baskets."
  ) +
  theme_report
```

A typical trip is worth **`r usd2(basket_median)`** (median), and the
average is **`r usd2(basket_mean)`** (SD `r usd2(basket_sd)`). Most
trips are modest, and a few large shops pull the average up. The chart
hides the top 1% of baskets (above `r usd0(cutoff)`) so the main shape
is visible, but the figures use every basket.

## Weekly sales over time

This chart shows total sales for each week. The sharp rise at the start
is not a spending boom. It happens because households enter the data
gradually, which the next two charts show. Weeks 1 to 19 are shaded as a
warm-up period.

```{r weekly-sales-line}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5.5
# Total sales for every week in the data
weekly_sales <- transactions %>%
  group_by(week_no) %>%
  summarise(weekly_sales = sum(sales_value))

# Summary numbers and the best and worst weeks, used for labels
weekly_mean <- mean(weekly_sales$weekly_sales)
weekly_sd   <- sd(weekly_sales$weekly_sales)
peak_week   <- weekly_sales %>% slice_max(weekly_sales, n = 1)
low_week    <- weekly_sales %>% slice_min(weekly_sales, n = 1)

weekly_sales %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = week_no, y = weekly_sales)) +
  geom_line(colour = deeppurple, linewidth = 0.9) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = 19.5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = lavender, alpha = 0.25) +
  annotate("text", x = 10, y = Inf, vjust = 1.6,
           label = "Warm-up period\n(weeks 1 to 19)",
           colour = deeppurple, fontface = "bold", size = 4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE,
              colour = coral, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(data = peak_week, colour = lavender, size = 3.5) +
  geom_point(data = low_week, colour = coral, size = 3.5) +
  geom_label(data = peak_week, vjust = -0.7, colour = lavender, fontface = "bold",
             aes(label = paste0("Highest: ", usd0(weekly_sales), " (week ", week_no, ")"))) +
  geom_label(data = low_week, vjust = 1.7, colour = coral, fontface = "bold",
             aes(label = paste0("Lowest: ", usd0(weekly_sales), " (week ", week_no, ")"))) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.3, 0.2)), breaks = seq(0, 104, by = 13)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = usd0, expand = expansion(mult = c(0.12, 0.15))) +
  labs(
    title    = "Total sales per week",
    subtitle = "Sales rise sharply while households join the data, then level off",
    x        = "Week number",
    y        = "Total sales",
    caption  = "Dark purple line = weekly total; dashed coral line = smoothed trend; shaded area = warm-up weeks excluded from baseline comparisons."
  ) +
  theme_report
```

The next two charts split total sales into its two parts: how many
households shopped each week, and how much each of them spent.

```{r weekly-active-households-and-sales}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 8
# Count how many different households shopped in each week, and the sales per active household
active_households <- transactions %>%
  group_by(week_no) %>%
  summarise(
    active_households = n_distinct(household_key),
    weekly_sales      = sum(sales_value)
  ) %>%
  mutate(sales_per_active_household = weekly_sales / active_households)

# Summary numbers used in the chart subtitles
hh_mean <- mean(active_households$active_households)
hh_sd   <- sd(active_households$active_households)
sp_mean <- mean(active_households$sales_per_active_household)
sp_sd   <- sd(active_households$sales_per_active_household)

# Chart 1: how many households shopped each week
chart_active <- active_households %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = week_no, y = active_households)) +
  geom_line(colour = deeppurple, linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 104, by = 13)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = big, limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Households shopping each week",
    subtitle = paste0("Mean ", big(round(hh_mean)), " (SD ", big(round(hh_sd)), "); range ",
                      big(min(active_households$active_households)), " to ",
                      big(max(active_households$active_households))),
    x = "Week number", y = "Active households"
  ) +
  theme_report

# Chart 2: sales per active household each week
chart_per_household <- active_households %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = week_no, y = sales_per_active_household)) +
  geom_line(colour = coral, linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = deeppurple) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 104, by = 13)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = usd2, limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Sales per active household each week",
    subtitle = paste0("Mean ", usd2(sp_mean), " (SD ", usd2(sp_sd), "); range ",
                      usd2(min(active_households$sales_per_active_household)), " to ",
                      usd2(max(active_households$sales_per_active_household))),
    x = "Week number", y = "Sales per household"
  ) +
  theme_report

# Stack the two charts (patchwork is already loaded)
chart_active / chart_per_household
```

**Top chart:** the number of households shopping each week climbs from
**`r min(active_households$active_households)`** to about
**`r big(max(active_households$active_households))`** and levels off
around week 17. **Bottom chart:** sales per active household stay steady
at **`r usd2(sp_mean)`** (SD `r usd2(sp_sd)`), with only a gentle upward
drift (purple line). So the early rise in total sales comes from more
households appearing in the data, not from households spending more.
Weeks 1 to 19 are therefore excluded when comparing spend before and
during campaigns. Sales dip in the final weeks, so the last week may be
only partly recorded.

# 4. Campaigns

Before measuring any effect, we need to know what the campaigns were:
how many, what type, when they ran and how many households each one
targeted.

## Campaign overview

Lists each campaign with its type, timing and reach, in the order they
started. Weeks are worked out from the day numbers so they match the
weekly charts.

```{r campaign-overview}
# Count how many different households each campaign targeted
campaign_targets <- campaign_hh %>%
  group_by(campaign) %>%
  summarise(households_targeted = n_distinct(household_key))

# Join the counts to the campaign descriptions and work out weeks and length
campaign_overview <- campaign_desc %>%
  left_join(campaign_targets, by = "campaign") %>%
  mutate(
    start_week  = ceiling(start_day / 7),     # day 1 to 7 is week 1
    end_week    = ceiling(end_day / 7),
    length_days = end_day - start_day + 1
  ) %>%
  mutate(description = str_replace(description, "Type", "Type ")) %>% 
  arrange(start_day) %>%
  select(campaign, description, start_week, end_week, length_days, households_targeted)

# Display in kable
campaign_overview %>%
  kable(caption = "The campaigns in order of start date",
        col.names = c("Campaign", "Type", "Start week", "End week", "Length (days)", "Households targeted"),
        align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r", "r")) %>%
  style_table()
```

## Campaign types

The campaigns come in three types, labelled A, B and C. They differ in
how coupons were given out:

- **Type A:** each household in the campaign received 16 coupons, chosen
  from a pool of coupons according to what that household had bought
  before.
- **Type B and Type C:** every household in the campaign received all of
  the coupons for that campaign.

This matters for the analysis. Type A coupons were matched to each
household's past buying, so households may already have been likely to
buy those products. Results are therefore compared by campaign type as
well as overall.

```{r campaign-types}
# Summarise the campaigns by type: how many, how long, how many households targeted
campaign_types <- campaign_overview %>%
  group_by(description) %>%
  summarise(
    Campaigns                        = n(),
    `Length in days, mean (SD)`      = paste0(round(mean(length_days)), " (", round(sd(length_days)), ")"),
    `Households targeted, mean (SD)` = paste0(big(round(mean(households_targeted))), " (",
                                              big(round(sd(households_targeted))), ")")
  )

# Display in kable
campaign_types %>%
  kable(caption = "Campaigns by type", col.names = c("Type", "Campaigns", "Length in days, mean (SD)", "Households targeted, mean (SD)"),
        align = c("l", "r", "r", "r")) %>%
  style_table()
```

There were a total of **`r sum(campaign_types$Campaigns)`** campaigns:
**`r campaign_types$Campaigns[1]`** `r campaign_types$description[1]`,
**`r campaign_types$Campaigns[2]`** `r campaign_types$description[2]`
and **`r campaign_types$Campaigns[3]`** `r campaign_types$description[3]`. 

The highest average reach was for
**`r names(which.max(tapply(campaign_overview$households_targeted, campaign_overview$description, mean)))`**
campaigns, targeting an average of
**`r big(round(max(tapply(campaign_overview$households_targeted, campaign_overview$description, mean))))`**
households (SD
`r big(round(sd(campaign_overview$households_targeted[campaign_overview$description == names(which.max(tapply(campaign_overview$households_targeted, campaign_overview$description, mean)))])))`).

## Campaign timeline

Shows when each campaign ran against the warm-up period, so any campaign
that overlaps it stands out.

```{r campaign-timeline}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
# Order the campaigns by start date (earliest at the top)
campaign_timeline <- campaign_overview %>%
  mutate(campaign_label = factor(campaign, levels = rev(campaign)))

campaign_timeline %>%
  ggplot(aes(y = campaign_label)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = 19.5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = lavender, alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = start_week, xend = end_week, yend = campaign_label, colour = description),
               linewidth = 4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(deeppurple, coral, lavender, purple)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 104, by = 13)) +
  labs(
    title    = "When each campaign ran",
    subtitle = paste0(nrow(campaign_overview), " campaigns; shaded area = warm-up weeks 1 to 19"),
    x        = "Week number",
    y        = "Campaign",
    colour   = "Campaign type"
  ) +
  theme_report +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```


```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
# For each week, count how many campaigns were running at the same time
campaigns_per_week <- tibble(week_no = 1:102) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(campaigns_running = sum(campaign_overview$start_week <= week_no &
                                 campaign_overview$end_week   >= week_no)) %>%
  ungroup()

# Summary numbers for the subtitle (weeks from the first campaign onward)
since_first <- campaigns_per_week %>% filter(week_no >= min(campaign_overview$start_week))
overlap_mean <- mean(since_first$campaigns_running)
overlap_sd   <- sd(since_first$campaigns_running)

campaigns_per_week %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = week_no, y = campaigns_running)) +
  geom_col(fill = lavender, width = 0.9) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 104, by = 13)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 0:10, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.08))) +
  labs(
    title    = "How many campaigns ran at the same time",
    subtitle = paste0("From week ", min(campaign_overview$start_week), " onward: mean ",
                      round(overlap_mean, 1), " (SD ", round(overlap_sd, 1), ") campaigns per week; maximum ",
                      max(campaigns_per_week$campaigns_running)),
    x        = "Week number",
    y        = "Campaigns running"
  ) +
  theme_report

```


```{r}
# Campaigns that reached too few households give unstable results, so set a minimum
min_households <- 100

# Count the campaigns by type, and how many reached at least the minimum
campaign_eligibility <- campaign_overview %>%
  group_by(description) %>%
  summarise(
    Campaigns = n(),
    `Reached 100 or more households` = sum(households_targeted >= min_households)
  )

# Display in kable
campaign_eligibility %>%
  kable(caption = "Campaigns large enough to analyse",
        col.names = c("Type", "Campaigns", "Reached 100 or more households"),
        align = c("l", "r", "r")) %>%
  style_table()
```
